input: It is important to note that overtime working in the quality laboratory amounted to 6% of total paid hours over the course of last year. The laboratory currently employs a team of 15 full-time staff members, and it should be emphasised that this overtime is by no means distributed evenly throughout the year; instead, it is heavily concentrated in two distinct seasonal peaks. One option that has been considered in some detail is to replace half of the overtime with one additional hire, an option that would cost $82k per year on a fully loaded basis, with the half in question corresponding to 3% of paid hours. However, it is worth bearing in mind that a new hire would be paid for the full year, including the quieter months that fall between the two peaks, when no overtime arises at all, whereas the overtime cost itself is incurred only during the peak periods themselves. It should also be noted that the remaining half of the overtime would still remain in place under this option, so the peaks would continue to be worked partly on overtime even after the hire was made. Overall, the comparison is essentially between a fixed commitment of $82k per year and a flexible, variable cost that arises only when demand peaks, and the decision ultimately hinges on how intense those peaks are, how far behind the laboratory falls during them, and what the resulting delays mean for the wider work that depends on laboratory results.

The remaining half of the overtime stays in place under this option, because the hire replaces only half of it, and the peaks would still be worked partly on overtime. The case for the hire rests on the intensity of the peaks: how far the laboratory falls behind during them, and what the delay costs the work that waits on laboratory results. Peak intensity also decides whether one hire is enough, since a hire adds fixed capacity in every peak week. Those effects are not costed in the figures stated here.
